MAIN.summary: Every direct <g> child of the root character group is one block. The shallowest, cheapest criterion — good for simple characters or a quick overview.

details.depth: direct children of the root only
details.academic: Pedagogically the weakest of the five: it groups by the accident of how KanjiVG happened to nest a character's outermost <g> elements, not by any semantic or etymological boundary. Corpus-wide (11,456 KanjiVG files), 55.58% of MAIN's own blocks still contain further nameable sub-structure it never surfaces — the worst under-decomposition rate of any of the five criteria, including SUB1. Best suited to characters with no internal composition at all (e.g. 一/十/木), or as a cheap fallback rather than a teaching tool in its own right.

SUB1.summary: Descends each branch to the first labeled <g> (kvg:element or kvg:radical present) and stops there, skipping transparent structural wrapper groups along the way. Surfaces the radical plus each top-level semantic component.

details.academic: Closer to a traditional radical-plus-remainder split, but still under-decomposes often: 51.63% of SUB1's blocks (12,743 of 24,679 corpus-wide) contain further nested named structure that SUB1 never exposes because it stops at the first labeled group on a branch — e.g. for 導 (michibiku, 'to guide'), SUB1 stops at 道, hiding the 首/自/目/⻌ structure beneath it and yielding only 2 blocks (道, 寸) where a finer reading distinguishes at least 3–4 meaningful parts. Note KanjiVG's own kvg:radical flag is NOT the classical 214 Kangxi bushu system — it is KanjiVG's own tagging convention, only sometimes aligned with traditional radical boundaries (this alignment has not been formally verified against the canonical Kangxi radical list as part of this project).

SUB2.summary: Like SUB1, but allows one extra level of labeled descent past the first hit on each branch, surfacing one layer of finer detail without going all the way to maximal depth.

details.depth: first labeled group per branch, plus one further level where available
details.academic: An empirically-motivated compromise, not a rule derived from any named pedagogical theory. Cuts the corpus-wide under-decomposition ('swallowing') rate roughly in half versus SUB1 — from 51.63% to 20.26% — and for 76.55% of the corpus a single extra level already reaches the same depth as the fully unbounded SUBMAX criterion. Its main advantage over SUBMAX is legibility on complex/rare characters: SUBMAX's unbounded descent can fragment such characters into runs of near-identical single-stroke labels that read as KanjiVG's own stroke-bookkeeping rather than teaching-relevant parts, a degeneration SUB2's fixed one-level cap structurally avoids by never descending far enough to reach it.

SUBMAX.summary: Descends as deep as possible along every branch, stopping only at a true semantic leaf (a labeled group with no further labeled descendants). Surfaces every named sub-component KanjiVG's own tree encodes, at the cost of many small blocks for structurally complex characters.

details.depth: unbounded — every semantic leaf in the tree
details.academic: The ceiling of what KanjiVG's own tagging can express: by construction, 0% of SUBMAX's blocks contain further nested named structure (verified corpus-wide, not merely typical). This ceiling is real, not absolute, in two documented ways. First, KanjiVG's tagging is not internally consistent: the same named component is sometimes decomposed further in one character and not in another with no marker distinguishing the two (e.g. 至 is split into 厶+土 in 41 of its 63 corpus occurrences but left as one unit, 土 only, in the other 20, including in 屋 specifically) — 16.07% of all distinct component names in the corpus show this inconsistency, so SUBMAX's depth on any single character is a lower bound on what KanjiVG's data could in principle support, not a fixed property of the character itself. Second, at the highest end of structural complexity (about 2% of the corpus, concentrated in rare/complex characters such as 囓), unbounded descent degenerates into runs of repeated single-stroke labels that reflect stroke-count bookkeeping rather than a teaching-relevant unit — a case where 'more decomposed' stops being 'more useful.' No claim is made here about which stopping depth is pedagogically correct for a given teaching context; SUBMAX only guarantees maximal exposure of what KanjiVG itself encodes.

KRAD.summary: Uses KRADFILE, an independent EDRDG-maintained kanji-component dataset, to decide which named sub-components are teaching-relevant for a given kanji, instead of relying on how deep KanjiVG's own tagging happens to go. Falls back to SUBMAX for a kanji not covered by the bundled mapping.

details.depth: determined by an external component list per kanji, not by KanjiVG tagging depth
details.dataSource: KRADFILE (EDRDG) mapped onto KanjiVG kvg:element/kvg:original, bundled as src/kradData.json
details.fallback: SUBMAX (used automatically for a kanji with no usable KRAD mapping)
details.attribution: KRADFILE component data is Copyright 2001/2007 Michael Raine, James Breen and the Electronic Dictionary Research & Development Group (EDRDG), licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://www.edrdg.org/edrdg/licence.html). See https://www.edrdg.org/wiki/index.php/KANJIDIC_Project.
details.academic: KRADFILE's component vocabulary is deliberately more granular than the 214 classical Kangxi radicals — it is a corpus of empirically-identified visual/graphic units, not a lexicographic radical assignment, and should not be presented to learners as equivalent to traditional bushu classification. Cross-validated against KanjiVG (25,452 kanji-component pairs, 6,238 kanji): 80.0% of everything KRADFILE names has an identifiable counterpart in that kanji's own KanjiVG tree (62.3% by exact match, 1.6% via KanjiVG's own declared tagging variants, 16.0% by algorithmic/AI-assisted disambiguation against cross-character statistical patterns, reviewable in the project's docsNoGit/ research notes). Of the remaining 20%: 19.7 points are components KanjiVG's tagging of that specific file simply never names at any depth (the same tagging-inconsistency phenomenon noted under SUBMAX, now confirmed against a second, independently-compiled source rather than only observed within KanjiVG itself) — this is the case that produces this criterion's SUBMAX fallback for the affected kanji. A further narrow 0.3% affects characters concentrated in complex traditional (kyūjitai) forms (e.g. characters in the 齒/齊/我/喜/雚 families), where KanjiVG's own stroke-level representation of the character is structurally incompatible with a classical-radical reading rather than merely less detailed — these are excluded from the mapping outright rather than forced into a misleading match. Two statistically strong but ultimately spurious candidate matches (co-occurrence within a shared phonetic-family cluster, not genuine shape correspondence) were identified and deliberately rejected during construction of the bundled mapping; this is disclosed as a caution against treating high cross-character correlation alone as sufficient evidence of a real component match.

CHISE_MAIN.summary: Uses CHISE/IDS (Ideographic Description Sequences), a compositional decomposition notation maintained by the CHISE project, to decide which named sub-components are teaching-relevant for a given kanji — an academically-oriented alternative to KRADFILE. Stops each IDS branch at the first component that already matches a recognized KanjiVG element. Unlike every other criterion, its data is never bundled with the package: it is GPLv2-licensed and must be generated locally and passed in explicitly by the consumer as the chiseData option. Unlike KRAD, it does NOT silently fall back to SUBMAX: it throws if chiseData is not supplied, or for a kanji not covered by it, so a result is always genuinely CHISE_MAIN.

details.depth: determined by an external, recursively-expanded IDS decomposition per kanji (stopping at the first KanjiVG-recognized, non-noise component per branch), not by KanjiVG tagging depth
details.dataSource: CHISE IDS Database (chise.org), via the cjkvi/cjkvi-ids mirror (https://github.com/cjkvi/cjkvi-ids), mapped onto KanjiVG kvg:element/kvg:original. NEVER bundled with the DAKAISB npm package — generated locally by running `npm run fetch-chise` (chains tools/fetch-chise.mjs, tools/prepare-chise-phase3.mjs, tools/build-chise-mapping.mjs, tools/build-chise-data.mjs) and must be imported and passed in by the consumer as the chiseData config option. See README.md's colorCriteria: "CHISE_MAIN" section for the exact setup and import steps.
details.fallback: None — throws an Error if chiseData is not passed at all, or if the specific kanji has no entry in it. This is deliberately stricter than KRAD's automatic SUBMAX fallback: because chiseData is opt-in and trivially easy to simply omit, a silent substitution would be too easy to mistake for genuine CHISE_MAIN output. Callers who want a fallback (e.g. SUBMAX) must catch the error and choose one explicitly.
details.attribution: IDS data is derived from the CHISE project (https://www.chise.org/) via cjkvi/cjkvi-ids (https://github.com/cjkvi/cjkvi-ids), licensed under GPLv2. This is a different license family from DAKAISB itself (PolyForm Noncommercial) and from KanjiVG (CC BY-SA 3.0) / KRADFILE (CC BY-SA 4.0) — this is precisely why the generated chisedata/chise.json is never distributed as part of the npm package: anyone who runs the fetch script and uses the resulting file is subject to GPLv2 for that data specifically.
details.academic: CHISE/IDS is structurally a different kind of source from KRADFILE: it encodes a compositional decomposition tree via Unicode IDS operators (⿰⿱⿲...) rather than a flat per-kanji component list, and its raw decomposition depth is often shallower per level than KRADFILE's own granularity (e.g. 導 decomposes in one IDS step to 道+寸, with 道 itself further decomposable to 辶+首). CHISE_MAIN recursively expands each non-terminal IDS component but stops each branch at the first KanjiVG-recognized, non-noise component it reaches (a SUB1-style rule), deliberately gating expansion depth by what KanjiVG already tags — see "CHISE_SUBMAX" for the sibling criterion that expands to CHISE/IDS's own true leaves instead, independent of KanjiVG's tagging. This KanjiVG-gated approach was adopted after a deeper, SUBMAX-style 'keep expanding while further structure exists' rule was tried first and rejected as CHISE_MAIN's own expansion rule, because a small number of components (e.g. 土) have their own IDS entry decomposing them into raw strokes even though they are genuine, teaching-relevant KanjiVG elements, and unconstrained recursion produced results measurably deeper than KRADFILE's own reference mapping for the same kanji (verified directly: 屋 recursed to [尸,厶,十] under the deeper approach versus KRADFILE's own [土,尸,至]; the shallower, adopted rule instead yields [尸,至], comparable to but independently derived from KRADFILE's grouping). A small fixed blacklist of eight CJK stroke labels (一/丨/丿/丶/亅/匚/乙/匸) that are technically valid kvg:element values but empirically tag only isolated single strokes corpus-wide (≥50 occurrences, average own-path-count ≤1.3) is excluded from ever being treated as a stopping point, to avoid noise from KanjiVG's own low-level stroke bookkeeping. Cross-validated against KanjiVG (13,741 kanji-component pairs from an initial pass over 6,154+ kanji with a KanjiVG file): 90.2% resolved deterministically (89.4% by exact string match, 0.8% via KanjiVG's own declared kvg:original variants); of the remaining 1,346 unresolved (kanji, component) pairs spanning 195 distinct CHISE components, AI-assisted disambiguation against cross-character candidate-coverage statistics resolved 30.2% (406 occurrences) as agent-semantic matches (a real KanjiVG counterpart under a different label), left 52.5% (707 occurrences) as absent (the CHISE component genuinely has no named node in that kanji's own KanjiVG tree at any depth — the same cross-source tagging-inconsistency phenomenon documented under SUBMAX and KRAD, here confirmed against a third, independently-derived source), and flagged 17.3% (233 occurrences) as structural-mismatch, where CHISE and KanjiVG segment the character fundamentally differently rather than merely at different depths — the clearest case being 阝, whose IDS-derived occurrences split into a near-exact 67.7%/32.3% left-position/right-position ratio matching two positionally distinct KanjiVG components (阝 as こざとへん vs 阝 as おおざと) that CHISE's notation does not itself distinguish. The final bundled-at-generation-time mapping covers 6,154 kanji (94.2% of the KanjiVG corpus by presence, verified corpus-wide with zero stroke-count mismatches and zero empty blocks across all 11,456 KanjiVG files when chiseData is supplied).

CHISE_SUBMAX.summary: Same CHISE/IDS source and never-bundled data policy as CHISE_MAIN, but with a deeper, independently-expanded component set: each IDS branch is followed all the way to CHISE/IDS's own true leaves, without stopping early just because KanjiVG already tags some intermediate component. KanjiVG is used only afterwards, to find which group to color for each resulting leaf — never to decide how far the decomposition itself goes. Like CHISE_MAIN, throws (never falls back to SUBMAX) if chiseData is not supplied or the kanji isn't covered.

details.depth: determined by an external, recursively-expanded IDS decomposition per kanji, expanded to CHISE/IDS's own true leaves (self-decomposition or no further IDS entry) — NOT gated by KanjiVG's own tagging depth at any point during expansion
details.dataSource: CHISE IDS Database (chise.org), via the cjkvi/cjkvi-ids mirror (https://github.com/cjkvi/cjkvi-ids), expanded to true IDS leaves and then mapped onto KanjiVG kvg:element/kvg:original as a separate, later step. NEVER bundled with the DAKAISB npm package — generated locally by running `npm run fetch-chise-submax` and passed in by the consumer as the chiseData config option (a different file from CHISE_MAIN's — the two encode different component granularities for the same kanji and are not interchangeable). See README.md's colorCriteria: "CHISE_SUBMAX" section for the exact setup and import steps.
details.fallback: None — throws an Error if chiseData is not passed at all, or if the specific kanji has no entry in it, same policy as CHISE_MAIN and for the same reason (chiseData is opt-in and easy to omit; a silent SUBMAX substitution would be too easy to mistake for genuine output).
details.attribution: IDS data is derived from the CHISE project (https://www.chise.org/) via cjkvi/cjkvi-ids (https://github.com/cjkvi/cjkvi-ids), licensed under GPLv2 — same attribution and never-bundled rationale as CHISE_MAIN.
details.academic: CHISE_SUBMAX exists to test a specific methodological question raised during CHISE_MAIN's own construction: should a second, independently-compiled decomposition source (CHISE/IDS) be allowed to describe a kanji only as deep as KanjiVG's own tagging already goes, or should it be treated as authoritative in its own right and matched onto KanjiVG only afterward, purely to find where to apply each resulting color? CHISE_MAIN takes the first position (KanjiVG-gated expansion, by design — see its own academic note for why). CHISE_SUBMAX takes the second: IDS expansion runs to true leaves independent of KanjiVG, and only the resulting leaf set is matched against KanjiVG's kvg:element/kvg:original names, exactly as KRADFILE's own already-flat component list is matched for KRAD — this makes CHISE_SUBMAX methodologically closer to KRAD's matching pipeline than to CHISE_MAIN's KanjiVG-gated expansion, despite sharing CHISE_MAIN's runtime walk algorithm. Concretely deeper: expanding 屋 to true IDS leaves reaches 至's own further decomposition (至 → 𠫔+土 → ...) rather than stopping at 至 the way CHISE_MAIN and KRADFILE both do, surfacing 厶/十 as candidate leaf components CHISE_MAIN never attempts to match at all. Cross-validated against KanjiVG (303,931 total (kanji, CHISE-component) pairs from an initial pass over all 88,347 CHISE/IDS entries with any component, of which 19,364 pairs belong to a kanji with its own KanjiVG file — the remaining 93.6% have no KanjiVG counterpart file at all, since CHISE/IDS's character coverage is far broader than KanjiVG's ~11,456 files): of the 19,364 in-scope pairs, 62.9% resolved deterministically (61.9% by exact string match, 1.0% via KanjiVG's own declared kvg:original variants); of the remaining 7,189 unresolved pairs spanning 111 distinct CHISE_SUBMAX leaf components, AI-assisted disambiguation resolved 28.3% (2,031 occurrences) as agent-semantic matches, left 68.7% (4,939 occurrences) as absent — a markedly higher absent rate than CHISE_MAIN's 52.5%, consistent with true IDS leaves reaching past the depth KanjiVG's own tagging bothers to expose for many characters (e.g. 屋's own 厶/十, checked directly against KanjiVG's至-phonetic family 室/屋/握/渥, confirmed absent with no dispersed candidate above 55% host coverage) — and flagged 3.0% (219 occurrences) as structural-mismatch, including two structurally unrelated CHISE codepoints (龰 and 𤴔) that independently bottom out at the identical KanjiVG 疋+卜+人 three-way split, a stronger and more specific structural-disagreement signal than any single case found for CHISE_MAIN. The 阝 positional-ambiguity finding (left/right KanjiVG components CHISE/IDS notation doesn't itself distinguish) reproduced independently here, a third confirmation of the same phenomenon across KRAD, CHISE_MAIN, and CHISE_SUBMAX. The final bundled-at-generation-time mapping covers 6,035 kanji (92.5% of the KanjiVG corpus by presence, marginally lower than CHISE_MAIN's 94.2% — consistent with deeper, more granular components being somewhat less likely to have a clean 1:1 KanjiVG counterpart — verified corpus-wide with zero stroke-count mismatches and zero empty blocks across all 11,456 KanjiVG files when chiseData is supplied, and confirmed to throw for every one of the 855 uncovered kanji rather than silently substituting SUBMAX).
